node.idea: Black meets e4 with the pawn to e6 — the French. The plan today is aggressive: build toward the enemy king and see if the attack can land a checkmate.
The French again, and against it the plan is the Steinitz: the pawn to e5 for the Advance, but instead of the usual c3 to prop up d4, a very odd-looking treatment is coming.
The French, and the pawn to e5 sets up the Advance. What follows is the Nimzowitsch treatment — a dangerous line that teaches closed structures and positional chess as much as it wins games.
Black strikes with the pawn to c5, and here everyone and their brother plays c3 to shore up d4. Not today — giving that pawn away looks unthinkable, and that's exactly the point of the line.

Instead of the automatic c3 to prop up the chain, slip through the cracks with the knight to f3 — develop as if nothing were wrong and let Black ruin the pawn chain by capturing on d4. It looks utterly counter-intuitive, and that's the point.

The bishop's best square is d3, behind the pawn. The bishop to b5 is a paper tiger — Black just blocks with the bishop to d7 — whereas from d3 it eyes h7, so if Black castles kingside a Greek-gift sacrifice is always waiting.

Black lunges with the pawn to c4, and the bishop simply steps back to e2. In a closed centre you can afford to move the same piece twice — and White has provoked c4, which relieves all the pressure on d4 and hands White a free hand on the queenside.
Now break the chain at its links: the pawn to b3 leans on c4, and the pawn to a4 will lean on b5. Classic pawn play — put pressure on both pawns at once and dismantle the structure without delay.

The pawn to a4 hits b5, the base of the chain — and note the tactical detail: the defence ...a6 is futile, because after the trade on b5 Black can't recapture with the a-pawn without hanging the undefended rook on a8. Timing is everything; strike before Black consolidates.
Take the base first — the capture on b5 removes the linchpin of the chain. Only then does the pawn on c4 fall, and with it comes a permanent structural weakness.
After the trades resolve on c4, White has achieved exactly the plan: a long-term, permanent weakness on the queenside. The c4-pawn is a chronic target that isn't going anywhere.

Castle first — it's safe, because Black has no way to get at the d4-pawn, and the knight on f3 guards e5 so a capture there is impossible. Then the pawn to c3 secures d4, and only after those preliminaries does White set about winning c4.

Black tries the pawn to f6 to open the centre — but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development, so welcome it. Capture on f6 and pry open the e-file, right onto the chronic weakness on e6.
No need to force it — the controlled move is the rook to e1, keeping the queen back to guard d4 for now. With two weaknesses on e6 and c4 and no time to develop, Black simply cannot hold.
The king came out to f7 to defend e6, but the knight to g5 forks it with check and knocks it back. The pawn is won — though there's still technique to show with the king this exposed.

Black's king walks into the pin, and the clinical punish is the rook takes e6 with check — but the check is just a bonus. The real point is that next comes the pawn to d5, winning the knight on c6 because its defender is pinned, and the whole queenside can stay home.

The pawn to d5 is the game-winner — it wins the pinned knight, and once that minor piece falls the king is hunted down. White won't even need most of the queenside pieces; the already-active ones are that powerful.

The finish is straightforward attacking chess: after the capture on c6 with check the knight defends the rook — that detail matters — and the king is dragged to c7. The bishop to f4 checks, and after the block the queen takes on d6 with checkmate.

node.idea: Castle and accelerate — the rook is coming to e1 not to attack yet but to over-protect e5. Leave d4 alone, pile support behind the clamp, and let development do the talking.
The knight to h6 is the standard French rerouting — it's heading for f5. Don't capture it; taking only helps Black's structure and hands him the open lines he wants.

The knight to c3 — looking deeper, this stops the ...Nb4-d6 idea that would dig at the light bishop, and it develops toward the centre. Sometimes the useful move is simply the one that denies the opponent his plan.

Here is the move to burn into memory: with a knight on c3 and the enemy queen on b6, always look at the knight to a4. It hits the queen and the c5-pawn at once, and Black's whole queenside starts to wobble.

The knight takes on c5 and the bishop recaptures — and that's the real gain. When the dust settles Black's dark-squared bishop has been traded off, White owns the two bishops, and Black's position is positionally in shambles.

No rush to attack — the pawn to c3 guards the d4-square, a very typical, solid touch, and Black's ...Ng4 is nothing to fear because the queen to e2 and a later h3 simply shove it back. Play it positionally first.
The pawn to b4 isn't just a hit on the queen — it stakes out c5 as an outpost. Every tempo now buys an important square for the pieces, and the bishop already has its eye on that hole.

The bishop swings to d6, parking itself right in Black's gut and slicing down the diagonal. There was no hurry — but with everything else in place, planting it here is a fine way to finish the buildup.

Now for the concrete phase. Development is done, the bishop dominates, and Black's king is stuck in the centre with no castling in sight — so the knight jumps to g5 and the queen heads for h5. This is going for the throat.

node.idea: Bishop to d3, and the capture on d4 simply doesn't matter. The whole idea is to keep developing and let the e5-pawn do the cramping while Black spends moves on a pawn that was never the point.

Rather than castle, capture on c5. This reaches exactly the pawn structure Black would have got by taking on d4 — except here White never sacrificed the pawn, and the position is already unpleasant for Black.

The knight to c3 is the principled, most testing move. Two things frame the position: Black has no dark-squared bishop, so his remaining bishop is the bad one, and the Greek-gift sacrifice on h7 is quietly on the cards the moment Black castles kingside.
With the queen on c7, look at where the knight can go. The knight to b5 is thematic — it wants to sink its teeth into d6, the hole in Black's camp.

The knight to d6 with check, and it's not too late to strike — d6 is uncovered, so the knight jumps in without preparation. After the trade, a monster pawn lands on d6 and Black's position already stinks.

First eliminate the knight with the capture on g6 — because bishop to f4 straight away would just hang the bishop. Take, then play bishop f4: it supports the d6-pawn, and with no dark-squared bishop, Black has nothing to challenge it with.

Notice the extra point: recapturing wrecks Black's kingside pawns and opens the h-file, and if Black castles short he steps into an attack down it — while, other than the rook on h8, Black has no kingside firepower to make that file cut both ways.
The knight to g5 is prophylaxis and attack in one. Its main job is to stop ...f6 — because then e6 would hang — and at the same time it joins the hunt on Black's king.
Time for the rook lift — the rook to e3, ready to swing to h3 and join the queen against the king. The pieces are all pointing the same way; now they converge.
With the rook lifted, the queen comes to g4 and the threats mount — rook to h3 next, and the mating net tightens. Everything is in place; the attack plays itself.

node.idea: This time the knight to d2 — the Tarrasch, the line played for a lifetime. It straddles the bridge: not as theory-heavy as the knight to c3, not as dry as the Exchange, yet with real venom to crush an underprepared opponent.
Against the knight to f6 the pawn goes to e5 and the structure becomes an Advanced-French shape — Black's f6-knight is chased back and White has the familiar space clamp.
The bishop comes to d3, its most natural square, eyeing the kingside. Simple, principled development before the central tension arrives.
And here, unlike in the Nimzowitsch line, White does play the pawn to c3. Don't confuse this with the Advance proper — it's a common French structure, but the piece configurations are very different.
The tempting reply, the pawn to h3, only makes it worse — then ...g4 comes and can rip open the h-file, the last thing you want in front of your own king. Never meet g5 this way.

node.idea: The pawn to e5 gains space and kicks the knight, which tucks back to d7. Now the clamp is up and White has the familiar French space advantage.

Here is why d2 was worth blocking the bishop: when Black hits with c5, White answers with the pawn to c3 and keeps the centre fully intact. It's the best of both worlds — pieces develop, the d4-e5 chain holds, and the other knight will take over guarding d4.
The knight to f3 — the g-knight, not the natural-looking knight to b3. For decades this was thought inferior because d4 is hard to hold, but engines flipped the verdict: it's the more testing move.

And this is the modern question the computers asked: what if you simply don't defend d4 at all? Castle and let the pawn go — in return you get a lead in development, more space, and the e5-pawn clamping the centre.

This is the move that holds it all together — the knight to f3. After the queen grabs on d4 the bishop and pawns are hanging and the position would collapse without it, but the knight develops with tempo, driving the queen off before she can cash in. From here White must keep following up accurately, like in any d4-pawn gambit.

node.idea: This is the Rubinstein French — Black gives up the centre with the capture on e4 for a rock-solid, if slightly passive, structure. It can arrive through the Tarrasch or the Nc3 move order, and every e4-player has to know how to handle it.
Trading on f6 reaches the main tabia of the line. From here White has five or six reasonable setups — g3, the classical Bd3 — but the one with the best modern reputation is coming.

The move is the pawn to c3, and it's easy to misread as purely positional. Yes, it reinforces d4 — but it also opens the d1-a4 diagonal, and the check on a4 is a major resource in these positions as long as Black's king sits on e8.
The bishop to e3 develops with a point — it leans on c5, and the real threat is simply to capture there. A developing move that also poses a concrete question is worth two.

Now the knight to e5 — the perfect moment to centralise it. The check on a4 would achieve nothing, since Black just plays the bishop to d7 and you've only helped him develop; the knight on e5 is the real prize.

Leaning toward the capture on c5 — into an endgame rather than a middlegame. It's not clearly the best, but it poses Black an immediate dilemma: take on e3 and enter the ending, or not. Posing problems has value of its own.

Queens come off and the pawn recaptures on e3. Black has lost the right to castle, and while White's e-pawns are doubled, the c5-b4-c3 wall is about to strangle any queenside counterplay — an excellent structure to grind from.
Start with the knight to c4 — the move you want anyway. It's flexible, it discourages the bishop coming to f6 because the knight to d6 arrives with tempo, and it keeps every option open.
This c5-b4-c3 construction, which shows up from many openings, is superb at winding down all of Black's queenside counterplay. As long as that chain holds, Black simply can't get his pawns moving.

The king walks to d2 to shepherd the c3-pawn — because you shouldn't tie a heavy piece to a menial defensive job. The rook on d8 isn't dangerous, and the king, the piece not yet participating, is the perfect defender; its home is c2.

Get the bishop out first with the move to e2, heading for f3. When Black tries the bishop to d7 and c6 for the long diagonal, White meets it on f3 — a defended square from which the bishop pressures b7.

The pawn to a4, as planned — it prepares b5 and the advance of the queenside pawn majority. Meanwhile that light-squared bishop of Black's does nothing; judge a piece by what it actually achieves, not by how many squares it nominally covers.

The rook to d6 is a classic maneuver: place one heavy piece ahead on the file to clear the way for the other. And recapture on d6 with the knight, not the pawn — the pawn recapture hands Black a tempo, and keeping the current structure leaves his knight paralysed by the weak c3-pawn.
The pawn to h3 restricts Black's pawns and denies any ...g4 activity. There's no hurry — Black isn't threatening anything — so tighten the vice before converting.

Here's the tactic that wins a second pawn: the pawn to f4 knocks the bishop off e5, and after the trade White captures on f6 with check and comes around to collect on h5. It doesn't end there — the bishop will fight back to e5, and the knight is freed by walking the king to e4 to dislodge it.

children.idea: Before the king commits to e4, fix the queenside with the pawn to c4. That's the magic of the line: after the king comes to e4 and Black tries the bishop to c3 to win the b4-linchpin of the majority, the knight jumps to f4 with check and escapes — c4 first is what makes it work.

Now it's just too many passers. The pawn to c6 creates an outside passer on the a-file — the general rule is that a passed pawn wants to be as far from the enemy pieces as possible, and corner pawns are the hardest of all to stop.

node.idea: Black opens with the pawn to g6 — the Modern, not a French, though it will soon take on a French-shaped centre. Against it the plan is a broad pawn chain to blunt the fianchettoed bishop.

The pawn to c3 builds the chain, so the bishop on g7 is biting on granite — it stares at d4 but can't budge it. The one downside is that c3 denies the knight its natural c3-square; no problem, the knight simply develops to d2 instead.

Just like in the London, once you've built the little pawn house you put the bishop in its hole — the bishop to d3. Try to get the dark-squared pieces sorted before that knight commits, and otherwise just develop naturally.

Black plays the pawn to d5, and closing with e5 is a no-brainer. The move to g6 already weakened all the dark squares, and shutting the centre makes those squares far easier to target — this becomes a French-style Advance with an extra hole on f6.

When Black locks it further with the pawn to c4, that suits White perfectly — the queenside is sealed, the d4-pawn is under no real pressure, and White gets what amounts to a free hand to attack on the kingside.
The attack will aim at the dark squares Black conceded — above all f6 and e5. The job now is to route the b1-knight toward those holes, and everything is arranged around getting it there.
The rook to e1 looks odd, even bad — but its purpose is to vacate f1 for the knight. The route is knight to d2, to f1, then to e3 or g4, and on toward the f6-square.
The knight came to f5, and the bishop to g5 exploits its drawback: it hits the queen with tempo along the now-open diagonal, keeps the clamp on f6, and readies the pawn to g4 to chase the knight.
Black's pawn to f6 does White's work: after the trades the e5-square becomes a gaping weakness. Occupy it with a knight, not a rook — a rook is a poor blockader — and there's no rush to do it.
The knight to e3 keeps to the plan, eyeing g4 and then the e5-outpost. Flexible, unhurried — the square isn't going anywhere.

With total control of e5 there's no need to rush a piece onto it — nobody can contest it. Connect the rooks first, maybe double on the e-file, and stay patient; here the threat is stronger than the execution.
Before anything else, stop Black's one idea — the pawn to g5. The move to h4 does it; f4 would only weaken things by cutting the queen's diagonal. The h4 and g3 arrangement locks the kingside down.

Normally you'd keep the knight on e5, but concretely the capture on g4 transforms the advantage — the knight has done its job, and now the rook simply collects the pawn on e6, leaving White up material with that monster e5-square intact.

Don't reflexively retreat the rook — marinate on the position and remember the bishop kept on c2 all game. It rakes the diagonal toward h7, and that's why the rook can crash into g6 with decisive threats. Black resigns.

node.idea: The pawn to d4 is the Alapin's whole idea — build the classical centre. After the exchange, White recaptures with a pawn and stands on a broad, mobile centre.
Develop the knight to c3, adding a piece to the centre. When Black pins with the bishop on b4, the bishop to g5 is a natural follow-up, creating pressure of its own.

node.idea: When Black strikes with d5, take it with the pawn — do NOT push e5. Locking the centre with e5 would concede an inferior French where Black's light-squared bishop has already escaped outside the chain.
After the queen recaptures on d5, the position is the standard Alapin tabiya — reached here by the Nc6 move order, but the same familiar isolated-pawn battleground.

Capturing on c5 is double-edged: it allows Black to trade queens and drag White's king into the centre. Many players avoid it for that reason, but the resulting queenless middlegame is fully playable.
After the queens come off and the king recaptures on d1, the position turns sharp and technical — a queenless middlegame where accurate play, not memorised theory, decides.

node.idea: The pawn to e6 is a third-tier move — respectable but a notch below the main d5 and Nf6. Its interesting property is transpositional: after d4 it can funnel into the same structures as the main lines.
The traditional response is the pawn to d5. Many Black players are really bluffing White into locking the centre with e5 — but there is no need to oblige, and capturing keeps White better.

The traditional line: exchange in the centre so Black is left with an isolated queen pawn on d5. That lone pawn is the whole story of the middlegame — a strength in the attack, a weakness in the endgame.
The bishop check on b5 gains a tempo, and the plan behind it is clean: capture on c5 to leave Black with an isolated d-pawn, then blockade and pressure it for the rest of the game.

node.idea: Instead of the accelerated setup Black answers with the small pawn to d6 — the classical Sicilian move order, a window into how a grandmaster handles the opening he knows best.
The bishop checks from b5 — the Moscow, or Canal, Variation. Rather than the open Sicilian, White pins toward the king and invites a block.
